This extraordinarily low neonatal mass, derived from an egg diameter of roughly 0.75 millimeters, is typical of broadcast-spawning marine teleosts that produce large numbers of small propagules. The larvae are initially lecithotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. Growth proceeds rapidly during the juvenile phase, and individuals eventually attain a maximum total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters] as sexually mature adults. The species exhibits a relatively fast life history, achieving its asymptotic length within a few years under favorable oceanic conditions along the northwestern Atlantic shelf. Maximum somatic growth rates are sustained by a diet dominated by gelatinous zooplankton, ctenophores, and small crustaceans, which are seasonally abundant in the species' preferred habitat.

This pattern is common among short-lived, iteroparous pelagic fishes that face high adult mortality from predators and fishing pressure. Field collections indicate that most individuals are reproductively active by their second summer, having spent their first year predominantly growing to the size necessary for successful gamete production and spawning.

Reproductive output in Atlantic butterfish is substantial, reflecting its pelagic spawning strategy. The maximum lifespan of Atlantic butterfish has been determined through long-term capture-mark-recapture programs and otolith-based aging studies. Senescence in this species appears to manifest gradually after the third or fourth year, with a decline in somatic condition and reproductive output observed among the oldest individuals. This adult body mass is achieved through the sustained ingestion of energetically dilute prey, which requires a high daily feeding rate.
